title: Ta'ameya
subtitle: Egyptian fava bean falafel
excerpt: Egypt's version of falafel: made from dried fava beans rather than chickpeas, blended with herbs, spring onion, and spices, then fried until shatteringly crisp outside and bright green within. The classic Egyptian street food.
sourceNotes: Ta'ameya is the Egyptian predecessor to the chickpea falafel now widespread across the Middle East. Cross-referenced with Claudia Roden, The New Book of Middle Eastern Food (2000), and Anissa Helou, Feast (2018).

recipe.freezeNotes: Shaped, uncooked ta'ameya freeze well for up to 1 month. Fry from frozen, adding 2 extra minutes.
recipe.batchNotes: Doubles well. The soaked-fava mixture keeps in the fridge for up to 2 days before frying.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: The fava beans must soak overnight (8 hours minimum). The mixture can be made the day before and refrigerated.

content.text: Ta'ameya uses dried split fava beans that have been soaked overnight and processed raw, not cooked. This is the method: the raw soaked bean gives a coarser, crispier result than chickpea falafel. The green interior comes from the herbs blended through the mixture. Use dried split fava beans, not tinned; the texture is completely different.

items.prepNote: dried split fava beans (not tinned), soaked in cold water for 8 to 12 hours
thinned with lemon juice and water for dipping

content.text: Drain the soaked fava beans and pat dry. Pulse in a food processor with the spring onion, herbs, garlic, spices, and salt until the mixture is finely chopped and holds together when pressed. It should not be a smooth paste; some texture is correct.
Transfer to a bowl. Cover and refrigerate for at least 30 minutes. The mixture firms up and the flavours develop.
Just before frying, stir in the baking powder. Shape the mixture into small patties about 4 cm across and 1.5 cm thick. Press sesame seeds onto both sides.

Heat 5 cm of oil in a heavy-based pan to 175°C. Fry the ta'ameya in batches of 4 to 5 for 3 to 4 minutes, turning once, until deep golden brown. Remove with a slotted spoon and drain on kitchen paper.
Serve immediately in warmed pitta with tomato, and tahini sauce made by thinning tahini with lemon juice and water to a drizzleable consistency.

items.symptom: The ta'ameya fall apart in the oil
items.cause: Mixture too wet or baking powder added too early
items.fix: Add baking powder only just before frying. If the mixture is very wet, refrigerate for longer or add 1 tablespoon of flour.

items.symptom: The outside browns before the inside is cooked
items.fix: Reduce oil temperature to 170°C. Make the patties slightly thinner.
Use a generous handful of each herb. The green comes from the chlorophyll in the fresh herbs.
Fry a small test patty and taste before shaping the rest. Adjust cumin, salt, and chilli.

content.text: Ta'ameya predates the chickpea falafel that has become universal in the Middle East. Egyptians are emphatic that fava bean ta'ameya is the original form, and will often note that the switch to chickpeas happened outside Egypt. In Cairo, ta'ameya vendors open at dawn and sell out by mid-morning. It is a breakfast food as much as a lunch food, eaten stuffed into pitta with tomato and tahini sauce, washed down with sweet tea.
